strengths: The proposed reduction from the Childs et al. glued-trees oracle problem is conceptually strong and, if completed correctly, would establish a significant unconditional exponential query separation for a central linear-algebra problem.

The hard instance is especially compelling: the matrix is real symmetric, has at most four nonzeros per row and column, has polylogarithmic condition number in the matrix dimension, and uses the simple right-hand side e1.

The manuscript carefully matches the quantum output model with the classical task of sampling from an approximate solution, avoiding the inappropriate comparison with explicitly outputting the entire solution vector.

The construction of M and the simulation of entry and row/column sampling access using graph-oracle queries are intuitive and largely plausible. The subsequent parameter translation correctly aims to turn a 2^(n/6) graph-query lower bound into an N^(1/12) linear-system lower bound.
The motivation for choosing lambda just above sqrt(8), and the analysis relating the solution mass at the second root to the precision and condition number, provide useful technical insight.

The paper is generally self-contained and readable for a theoretical submission. It gives explicit constructions and derivations, so no experimental code or unavailable data are needed for reproduction. The work raises no material research-ethics concerns.
weaknesses: The proof of the central spectral Lemma 1 contains a fundamental gap. Observation 2 claims that every eigenvalue of A has a nonzero layered eigenvector, but its construction averages an arbitrary eigenvector over each level. All of these averages can be zero, yielding the zero vector rather than an eigenvector. Equitable-partition averaging only preserves the projection onto the layered subspace; it does not imply that every eigenspace intersects that subspace nontrivially. Consequently, the subsequent recurrence analyzes only layered eigenvectors and does not rule out non-layered eigenvalues in (sqrt(8), 3-2^(-n)].

Lemma 1 is essential: without excluding those non-layered eigenvalues, lambda I-A may have a singular value much smaller than gamma, so the claimed O(log^2 N) condition number and hence the exponential quantum-classical separation do not follow. A separate bound on the spectrum orthogonal to the layered subspace may exist, but it is absent and would require substantial new argument rather than a local algebraic correction.

The SQ(M) simulation is not fully specified. The access definition includes querying every row/column norm and the norms associated with r(M) and c(M), but the simulation only explicitly discusses entry queries and sampling. These quantities appear recoverable with constant oracle cost or from known graph statistics, yet this should be stated and included in the query accounting.

The replacement of the exact norm-weighted distribution for sampling rows and columns by a uniform distribution is argued only through conditioning on not selecting a root. A formal coupling or total-variation calculation is needed, including the discrepancy between the true and simulated probabilities of the two root rows; the stated 2T·2^(-2n) loss is not rigorously derived as written.

The QIC problem statement does not clearly specify algorithmic failure probability, whether the approximation vector may depend on internal randomness, or the success convention for randomized preprocessing. These details matter when converting the sampler into an algorithm contradicting the bounded-success glued-trees lower bound.

The significance and originality would be very high if the theorem were established, but the current manuscript cannot support its headline claim because the missing spectral argument sits at the core of the proof. The result also applies only at the stringent precision epsilon=O(log^(-2.5) N), which limits its reach and deserves clearer treatment as a limitation.

The related-work discussion and bibliography appear to stop around 2024. For an ICML 2026 submission, the claim of being the first such separation requires an updated comparison with relevant 2025-2026 work.

strengths: The problem is significant: an unconditional exponential separation between quantum and quantum-inspired classical algorithms for sparse, well-conditioned linear systems would be an important theoretical result.

The proposed reduction from the Childs et al. glued-trees oracle problem is conceptually appealing. The construction is sparse, uses the simple right-hand side e1, and clearly explains how the claimed n^(1/12) lower bound follows from the exponential glued-trees bound.

The exposition is generally self-contained and provides useful intuition for choosing lambda near sqrt(8), including the tradeoff between conditioning and probability mass at the second root. No material research-ethics concerns arise.
weaknesses: The central spectral argument is invalid. Observation 2 claims that every eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix has a layered eigenvector. Averaging an eigenvector within each level does preserve the eigenvalue only when the averaged vector is nonzero; for eigenvectors whose coordinates sum to zero on every level, the result is the zero vector. Such non-layered eigenspaces are entirely possible for this equitable level partition. The proof overlooks this case.

Consequently, Section 2.2 analyzes only the spectrum on the low-dimensional layered subspace and does not rule out non-layered eigenvalues in (sqrt(8), 3-2^(-n)]. Lemma 1 is therefore unproved. This is decisive because Lemma 1 supplies the lower bound on the smallest singular value of B=lambda I-A and hence the claimed polylogarithmic condition number.

The claimed universal form of Lemma 1 is also doubtful for an arbitrary alternating cycle: the cycle can be arranged to create highly structured or weakly connected regions, whereas no expansion or non-layered spectral analysis is provided. If the intended statement is probabilistic for a uniformly random cycle, it requires a new high-probability spectral theorem and an argument that conditioning on the good event preserves the glued-trees query lower bound.

Without the condition-number guarantee, the construction does not establish an exponential quantum/classical separation: the quantum benchmark depends directly on kappa, so the paper's headline theorem and significance claim do not follow from the current proof.

The manuscript is readable, but its repeated assertion that Lemma 1 has been proved obscures the distinction between the quotient/layered spectrum and the full adjacency spectrum. Reproducibility is limited by this mathematical gap rather than by missing code or experiments; this is a theorem paper, but independent verification of the central claim fails at Observation 2. The paper also lacks a dedicated limitations discussion and presents the result as unconditional without acknowledging the required spectral assumption.
